speaker: Kelsey Hightower
title: Kubernetes and retiring at the top with Kelsey Hightower
question: In tech startups, why do standard equity-only advisory roles so rarely pay off for individual software engineers?
guest: When I first started doing startup advisory, it felt like an exact waste of time. VCs have large amounts of money, so they can invest in a thousand companies and ideally one of them will return the entire fund. When you and I do angel investing or advisory, you typically take advisory shares, and 99.9 percent of the time they're worth absolutely nothing. First, you're going to get diluted to hell and back, especially when you get shares that are way low on the totem pole. Second, you often don't even know how the taxes work on them—you may exercise them in the wrong way and end up paying money out of pocket while getting nothing in the end. I also used to think you could advise a startup for four years, which makes no sense from experience. Advisory is really only good for about a year at a time because it should make a real impact, not four years of superficial check-ins—so instead of four-year vesting, I ask for one year, no cliff, and a long exercise window.

points.core: Individual advisors lack the massive portfolio scale VCs need for power-law returns.
points.note: Accept: VCs invest across hundreds or thousands of startups so one outlier returns the fund, whereas individuals hold too few bets. Do not credit: generic claims that 'most startups fail'.

points.core: Advisory shares sit low in the preference stack under heavy future dilution.
points.note: Accept: severe dilution across funding rounds or common/subordinated share priority wiping out advisor payouts. Do not credit: surface mention of 'equity is risky' without dilution or liquidation hierarchy.

points.core: Mismanaged option exercise triggers out-of-pocket tax bills on ultimately worthless shares.
points.note: Accept: AMT or tax liability from exercising options on illiquid stock that later goes to zero. Do not credit: generic advice to 'hire a tax lawyer'.

points.core: Multi-year vesting mismatches the short one-year window where advisory creates real impact.
points.note: Accept: four-year schedules drag past the stage-specific transition where an advisor actually helps. Do not credit: generic complaints about long vesting schedules without tying them to advisory impact duration.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Mostly because the math is stacked against them: a tiny slice of a high-variance asset, held from the weakest position on the cap table.

Typical advisor grants are about 0.1–1% of an early-stage company, vesting over roughly two years. Most startups fail or return little, so the expected value starts low. Even in the successes, that stake is diluted across several funding rounds, and it sits as common stock behind investors' liquidation preferences, so a modest acquisition can pay preferred holders fully while common gets almost nothing.

Liquidity is another problem. Exits often take seven to ten years, and advisors usually hold options that must be exercised (with cash and possible tax costs) within a limited window after the relationship ends, for shares they can't sell.

Engineers are also at a specific disadvantage. Advisory equity best rewards people who bring introductions, customers, or fundraising credibility; an engineer's contribution tends to be actual work, which is worth much more as paid consulting. And a single engineer typically holds one or two such positions, whereas investors rely on dozens of bets to catch the rare outlier.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Standard equity-only advisory roles rarely pay off for software engineers because microscopic, illiquid grants collide with adverse selection and unpaid scope creep. Under standard frameworks like the FAST agreement, advisors typically receive just 0.1% to 0.25% in common stock options vesting over two years. Because most startups fail—and surviving ones layer on heavy dilution and investor liquidation preferences—common shares often yield nothing even in modest acquisitions. Advisors also face exercise costs, decade-long illiquidity, and less favorable non-qualified stock option tax treatment.

Meanwhile, adverse selection skews the opportunity pool: well-capitalized startups with strong technical founders rarely trade equity for engineering guidance, meaning offers disproportionately come from cash-strapped teams lacking technical leadership. Consequently, expectations frequently drift from brief monthly check-ins into hands-on architecture work, debugging, or unpaid fractional CTO labor. Measured against market consulting rates, trading specialized engineering hours for a tiny, subordinated slice of high-risk equity almost always delivers a poor expected return unless the company achieves a rare outlier exit.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Standard advisory grants usually pay off only in an unusually large exit, and most startups never get there. Advisors typically get between 0.1% and 1% of the company, usually as common stock or options that vest over one to two years. Each funding round dilutes that stake, often cutting it in half or more by the time of an exit.

Most startups fail or are sold for modest amounts. Investors' liquidation preferences are paid before common shareholders get anything, so a "successful" acquisition can still leave advisors with close to nothing. Exits also tend to take seven to ten years, and the shares can't be sold in the meantime.

Options add their own problems. Many expire about 90 days after the advisor stops working with the company, which forces a choice between paying to exercise, sometimes with a tax bill, and losing the options. Advisory relationships also tend to fade before the grant fully vests.

Finally, founders tend to value an engineer's hands-on technical advice less than investor introductions or domain expertise, so engineers usually get grants at the low end of the range.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Standard equity-only advisory roles rarely pay off because the math is stacked against small common-stock holders at every stage. First, advisor grants are tiny—typically 0.1% to 0.5%—and most early-stage startups either fail outright or never reach a liquidity event. Second, even if the company survives and raises venture capital, subsequent funding rounds heavily dilute that stake, while investors' liquidation preferences ensure preferred shareholders get paid first, often wiping out common equity in modest exits. Third, advisors are usually granted non-qualified stock options rather than outright shares. Once the typical two-year vesting schedule ends, a standard 90-day post-termination exercise window often forces engineers to either spend real cash—and potentially trigger taxes—to buy illiquid paper or forfeit their vested options altogether. Finally, because advisory roles are unpaid, the opportunity cost is steep: engineers are trading valuable time that could earn guaranteed cash consulting rates for a lottery ticket with poor odds and years of illiquidity.

The engineer gives up time now in exchange for a small stake that may never turn into cash. Many startups never reach an exit that pays common shareholders. Even when a company is sold, fundraising may have diluted the advisor’s stake, and investors’ liquidation preferences can leave little for common shareholders. A high paper valuation tells you little about what the advisor will actually receive.

The engineer also has limited control over the outcome. A few hours of advice can help a team avoid costly mistakes, but the founders decide what to act on, and the payoff still depends on years of execution, fundraising, and market timing. Meanwhile, a light advisory commitment can grow into recurring calls, code reviews, and recruiting help. For an individual engineer, those hours come out of paid work, career development, or personal time. A venture fund can spread the risk across dozens of bets. An engineer with a handful of advisory roles has far fewer chances for one big win to make up for the rest.

The time you spend advising is certain, while the payout depends on several things going right. A startup typically offers an individual advisor a small equity grant that vests over time. Even if it vests in full, later funding rounds can dilute your stake. The company might fail or stay private for years, and even a sale can leave little for common shareholders once investors receive their contractual payouts.

The tradeoff is especially sharp for software engineers. A request for occasional advice can turn into debugging, architecture reviews, or hands-on implementation. Those hours have a market rate, but doing more work doesn’t automatically increase your grant. You also have limited control over the hiring, fundraising, and sales decisions that determine what your equity will be worth. An exceptional outcome can pay well, but a small stake in one company rarely compensates reliably for cash income you could earn with the same time.
